# Race, Ethnicity, Sex, and Socioeconomic Disparities in Anticoagulation for Atrial Fibrillation: A Narrative Review of Contemporary Literature

**Authors:** Danielle J. Daly; Utibe R. Essien; Marcela G. del Carmen; Benjamin Scirica; Adam N. Berman; Jen Searl Como; Jason H. Wasfy

**Affiliations:** 1Population Health Management, Performance Analysis and Improvement Unit, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA | 2Center for Health Equity Research and Promotion, VA Pittsburgh Healthcare System, Pittsburgh, PA | 3Division of General Internal Medicine, University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, Pittsburgh, PA | 4Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, Boston, MA | 5Center for Surgery and Public Health, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 6Division of Gynecologic Oncology, Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology and Reproductive Biology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA, USA | 7Massachusetts General Physicians Organization, Boston, MA | 8Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA | 9Cardiology Division, Department of Medicine, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA | 10Division of Cardiovascular Medicine, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Boston, MA

## Abstract

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most prevalent arrhythmia in the United States and is responsible for 1 in 7 ischemic strokes. While anticoagulation is effective at preventing strokes, prior work has highlighted significant disparities in anticoagulation prescribing. Furthermore, racial, ethnic, sex, and socioeconomic disparities in AF outcomes have been described. As such, we aimed to review recent data on disparities with respect to anticoagulation for AF published between January 2018 and February 2021. The search string consisted of 7 phrases that combined AF, anticoagulation, and disparities involving sex, race, ethnicity, income, socioeconomic status (SES), and access to care and identified 13 relevant articles. The aggregate data demonstrated that Black patients were less likely to be prescribed anticoagulation than patients of other racial/ethnic groups. Additionally, Black patients were more likely to be prescribed warfarin instead of direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) despite evidence that DOACs are safer and better tolerated. Lower-income patients and patients with less education were also less likely to receive DOACs. Some studies found that women were less likely to be anticoagulated than men even when their estimated stroke risk was higher, although other studies did not show sex-based differences. Building upon prior work, our study demonstrates that racial and ethnic disparities have persisted in the management of AF. Additionally, we our work highlights that there are significant disparities in anticoagulation management for AF associated with sex, income, and education. More work is needed to identify mechanisms for these disparities and identify potential solutions to achieve pharmacoequity.

## Introduction:

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a common arrythmia, affecting 9% of Americans over the age of 80 and is responsible for nearly 1 in 7 ischemic strokes.1,2,3 Worldwide, more than 37 million individuals are estimated to have AF.4 As such, risk assessment and potential therapy for stroke prevention are strongly recommended by clinical guidelines.3 For eligible patients, oral anticoagulation (OAC) is the standard of care for stroke prevention in individuals who are at high risk of AF related thromboembolism. 5 In order to determine if a patient may derive a net benefit from anticoagulation, clinicians must weigh risk for ischemic stroke versus risk for major bleeding.6–8

Historically, patients were prescribed warfarin – a vitamin K antagonist – for anticoagulation.9 Within the last decade, the introduction of direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) such as apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban, and rivaroxaban have changed the landscape of pharmacotherapy for anticoagulation. Landmark trials have demonstrated that DOACs are effective at preventing strokes and have lower bleeding risks than warfarin, leading to a decrease in the use of warfarin.9 Furthermore, recent cardiovascular guidelines now recommend DOAC use over warfarin in patients with AF at risk for ischemic stroke.7

Previous literature has highlighted disparities in overall OAC prescribing, type of anticoagulant chosen, and adherence to anticoagulation across different patient populations.10 This includes reports of disparate anticoagulation prescribing by race and ethnicity, sex, and socioeconomic factors.11–18 In a systematic literature review from 2018 that focused on race and ethnicity, Ugowe et al. examined racial and ethnic disparities in AF epidemiology, management, and outcomes in studies published prior to 2018.13 Given the rise in DOAC utilization, updated guidelines favoring DOAC use, and important research published over the last several years, it is critical to review these findings to determine if disparities have persisted.19 In addition, it is important to evaluate if these racial and ethnic disparities extend to other areas such as sex and socioeconomic status as prior work has demonstrated these differences.

In that context, the purpose of this work is to review the literature on disparities in anticoagulation for AF published since 2017. This narrative review will focus on anticoagulation for AF and will investigate disparities associated with race, ethnicity, sex, and socioeconomic status.

## Methods:

This narrative review used the PubMed database to identify peer-reviewed articles that analyze disparities in anticoagulation for AF patients with respect to race and ethnicity, sex, socioeconomic status (including education, income, and location of receiving care). The scope of this work does not include other AF-related disparities related to outcomes or efficacy of anticoagulant use (such as time in therapeutic range, a measure associated with warfarin use). One reviewer (Danielle Daly) independently ran search terms and collected subsequent analysis. We included both US and non-US-based studies. We limited our search to articles published after January 1, 2018 and before February 1, 2021, without limitations on when the data were generated. Due to limitations in reporting and clarity of definitions, we were not able to make the distinction between sex and gender. All articles included were available in English. The search string for the review consisted of seven phrases that included atrial fibrillation, anticoagulation, and forms of disparities. The phrases were: “health disparities in atrial fibrillation treatment,” “disparities in atrial fibrillation anticoagulation,” “racial disparities in atrial fibrillation anticoagulation,” “sex disparities in atrial fibrillation anticoagulation,” “disparities in atrial fibrillation control anticoagulation,” “equity in atrial fibrillation anticoagulation,” “socioeconomic disparities in atrial fibrillation anticoagulation” and “disparities atrial fibrillation anticoagulation adherence.” There were a total of 189 search results reviewed (Figure 1). Articles were excluded if they did not have relevant information about anticoagulation as a treatment for embolic prevention in AF. Other articles were excluded for focusing primarily on efficacy, outcome measures, or other conditions besides AF. Additional articles were excluded for lack of information or data describing disparities. From there, a total of 13 sources were used in this review. These results were then reviewed and synthesized to report findings within each body of work. Since this work did not analyze patient data, it was exempt from review from the Institutional Review Board at Mass General Brigham.

## Results:

Of 189 screened records, 4 were excluded for being reviews, 59 were excluded for lack of inclusion of anticoagulation as AF treatment, 46 were excluded for using anticoagulation as a treatment for a diagnosis other than AF, 33 were excluded for focusing on outcomes or efficacy which was out of the scope of this work, and 66 were excluded for a lack of information surrounding disparities (Figure 1). Many articles fell into multiple exclusion categories. In the final analysis, 13 studies met the inclusion criteria for this review.

### Racial and Ethnic Disparities in Anticoagulation Initiation and Quality

Seven studies published after 2017 provide evidence of racial and ethnic disparities in anticoagulation use in AF. These results include differences in overall prescription of anticoagulation and type of anticoagulant used.

An article from Essien et al. measured disparities in the use of anticoagulation across different races and ethnicities.20 The authors used the US-based Outcome Registry for Better Informed Treatment of Atrial Fibrillation II (ORBIT-AF II) to classify differences in anticoagulation for both DOAC and warfarin therapy by race and ethnicity in patients newly diagnosed with AF.20 The study examined 12,417 patients across 244 medical practices who were diagnosed with new AF from February 2013 to July 2016.20 They observed that 88.9% of White patients were anticoagulated with either warfarin or a DOAC as compared to 84.2% for Black patients (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.75 [95% CI, 0.56, 0.99]).20 DOACs were used more frequently than warfarin for White patients (85.2%) compared to Black patients (77.8%) with an aOR of 0.63 [95% CI, 0.49–0.83].20 These differences persisted even after adjusting for socioeconomic factors including income, educational level, and insurance status.20 There were no statistical differences in anticoagulant prescribing between White and Hispanic patients. Notably, Black patients were less likely to receive anticoagulation than White patients especially when they had a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 2 or higher at 67.5% and 77.0 % respectively, with a nearly 10% difference observed in DOAC prescribing between these two groups.20

A separate study from Essien et al. of Medicare beneficiaries found that the initiation of anticoagulation is lower in Black patients. Additionally, Black patients were less likely to be initiated on DOACs, with no significant difference between White and Hispanic patients.21 The study examined patients who were billed for incident nonvalvular AF through a randomized sample of Medicare beneficiaries from January 2013 through December 2014.21 The study sample included 42,952 patients, of whom 41.8% were women, 7.8% were Black, and 4.6% were Hispanic.21 The authors reported that overall anticoagulation initiation across all groups was low at 49.5% including 50.3 % of White patients, 46.2% of Black patients, and 45.5% of Hispanic patients.21 Of those anticoagulated, 58.1% initiated warfarin and 48.9% initiated a DOAC.21 Within these groups, DOACs were initiated in 42.9% of White patients, but in only 29.4% of Black patients (aOR 0.75; 95% CI, 0.66–0.85).21 The differences associated with race persisted after adjusting for socioeconomic status.21

An electronic health record study based in 11 healthcare centers within the Northwestern Medicine health system in Chicago, IL also assessed racial and ethnic differences in the use of anticoagulants for people with AF.22 They found that Black, Hispanic, and Asian patients were less likely to receive any anticoagulant compared to White patients (respective aORs 0.69, 0.74, 0.75).22 The study found low overall anticoagulation rates, with only 48.7% of overall participants receiving anticoagulation when their CHA2DS2-VASc score was 2 or higher, including 49.8% White, 39.8% Black, 41.3% Hispanic, 41.5 % Asian.22

The Florida Puerto Rico Atrial Fibrillation (“FLiPER-AF”) study examined anticoagulation data for patients with AF from 86 hospitals in Florida and Puerto Rico from 2010 to 2016.23 The study population consisted of 24,040 individuals with AF hospitalized for ischemic stroke including 54% women, of whom 74% were White, 10% were Black, and 16% were Hispanic (12% from Florida, 4% from Puerto Rico).23 Women in the study were 5 years older than men, with a mean age of 81, and had a higher prevalence of prior stroke, higher calculated stroke risk, and hypertension.23 Even though Black patients only consisted of 10% of the study sample, 35.2% were discharged with warfarin as opposed to DOACs for example compared to 31% of White patients (p < 0.05).23 25.8% of Florida Hispanic patients and 29.8% of Puerto Rico Hispanic patients were also discharged with warfarin.23 In this analysis, Hispanic patients in Florida and Puerto Rico at least were most likely to be discharged with DOAC compared to White and Black patients (OR, 2.5; 95% CI, 1.54–4.07; P=0.0002).23

An article by Kim, Xu, and Puckrein using Medicare claims data from 2000–2010 focused on disparities in clinical outcomes after using warfarin but also included information on disparities in rates of prescription of anticoagulation.24 In 2000, 38.1% of White patients, 28.4% of Black patients, 32.0% of Hispanic patients, 31.9% of Asian patients were prescribed warfarin for AF.24 In 2007 47.3% of White patients, 38.9% of Black patients, 42.9% of Hispanic patients, 31.9% of Asian patients were prescribed warfarin.24 Given the time period of data, DOAC use was not reported.24

A 5-year retrospective, longitudinal cohort study from 2010 to 2014 utilized the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS) to examine disparities in anticoagulation use.25 MEPS collected general healthcare data related to prescription drug use, costs, and diagnosis in the US. The authors found that non-Hispanic White patients had the highest rate of anticoagulant use (43.3%), and non-Hispanic Black patients were anticoagulated at half that rate (20.8%).25

While there are disparities in OAC prescribing between White and Black patients, such disparities may not always translate to other racial and ethnic groups. An analysis by Gu et al. specifically examined racial differences in anticoagulation between White patients and Asian patients and found that the rates of anticoagulation were similar between those two groups.26 The study noted that the Asian patients had lower CHA2DS2-VASc scores than the White patients.26 Additionally, they had a lower bleeding risk, as measured by HAS BLED score.26 There was no difference between White and Asian patients in terms of receiving OAC generally (OR: 0.97, 95% CI 0.93–1.01) or DOAC specifically (OR: 1.04. 95% CI: 1.00–1.09). 26

### Sex Disparities in Anticoagulation

Six papers were identified that report on sex disparities in anticoagulation for AF since 2017.24,27–30

Rodwin et al. reported data that included information about sex and found higher rates of OAC in men than in women.25 Specifically, 47% of men were anticoagulated in the study, as compared to 34% of women.25

Kim, Xu, and Puckrein also presented data related to sex differences in anticoagulation.24 The study notes that women are 4.4% less likely to be prescribed warfarin during the study time period, despite similar rates of AF presentation.24 Rates of warfarin use increased in women throughout the study period, which was prior to widespread use to DOACs.24

Essien et al. found that women had significantly lower odds of initiating any anticoagulation when compared to men in their study of Medicare recipients (aOR 0.59, 95% CI 0.55–0.64) but did not find a difference in DOAC prescribing patterns between men and women (aOR 0.98, 95% CI 0.88–1.10).21

Yong et al. found that women are less likely to receive anticoagulation compared to men even when having a higher calculated risk of stroke.27 Among the 358,649 patients studied from a national commercial claims database, women received OAC 3% less than men overall.27 Specifically, women received 5.3% less anticoagulation with warfarin and 1.5% less anticoagulation with a DOAC (P<0.0001). Even further, when adjusting for only high-risk patients with CHA2DS2-VASc greater than or equal to 4, women were anticoagulated at 49% versus men at 53% (P<0.0001).27

In contrast, one study using data from the OptumLab Data Warehouse found that women had higher rates of DOAC use over warfarin than men.30 The study looked at a total of 112,187 patients over the years of 2010–2017.30 At the beginning of the study, more women were prescribed warfarin than men, but with the increase of DOAC use, women started DOACs more often than men.30 (odds ratio = 1.19; 95% confidence interval = 1.14–1.25)

A study based in China also investigated sex differences in OAC prescribing.28 The study found a trend toward differences in anticoagulation between men and women, but only those under the age of 75.28 When adjusting for age, men were still more likely to receive OAC than women. The study reported that 32.1% of men under the age of 75 were prescribed OAC versus 30.1% women under 75 received OAC (P=0.081).28 Notably, however, there was no significant difference in OAC prescribing between women and men older than 75 (36.4% vs. 35.3%, P=0.7).28

### Socioeconomic Factors and Anticoagulation

The three studies included in this review assessed differences in anticoagulation characterized by socioeconomic status, includes factors such as education, income, and geography.31

An article by Zhu et al. found that warfarin is used more frequently than DOAC in patients with lower socioeconomic status.30 Those with high school and some college education made up 88.9% of warfarin users, while those with bachelor’s degrees and above made up 8.9% of warfarin users.30 73.5% of warfarin users lived in the southern or midwestern regions of the US. Furthermore, warfarin use was more common in low household net worth at 44.7% as compared to 27.1% of medium household net worth and 19.1% of high household net worth.30

One article examined socioeconomic status and education in urban areas in Sweden to determine the differential rates of DOACs and warfarin use in AF treatment.32 They found that higher education is associated with DOAC use over warfarin.32 In the study population of 68,000 patients, those who lived in rural areas were twice as likely to receive DOACs compared to warfarin.32 Additionally, the investigators found that patients with higher education, higher paying jobs, higher income, and higher-level employment were also more likely to be prescribed DOAC.32

There may also be differences in anticoagulation prescribing patterns related to access to clinical care. An article by Rangnekar et al. assessed differences in anticoagulation for AF between emergency department and outpatient settings.33 Patients presenting to the ED experienced 40% more cases of under-anticoagulation compared to outpatient cardiology participants.33 Overall, patients presenting to the ED with AF experienced inappropriate OAC management 47% more than patients managed through outpatient cardiology care.33

## Discussion:

In this review, we report persistent disparities in anticoagulation prescribing patterns for patients with AF. Such disparities are particularly notable regarding race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status. Disparities are present for sex as well, but less consistently demonstrated and smaller in magnitude. Importantly, these disparities have persisted and even widened over the last decade with increasing utilization of DOACs. Our analysis extends prior work by assessing 13 papers not previously summarized, encompassing a broader range of sociodemographic disparities.13

Our review demonstrated that Black patients were less likely to be prescribed OAC than other patients, especially compared to White and Asian patients even when their CHA2DS2-VASc stroke risk scores were similar – particularly important since they are known to have higher rates of complication from AF.21–24,34 When they were prescribed OAC, Black patients were also less likely to be prescribed DOACs compared to White patients.20,21,23 Unsurprisingly, increased use of warfarin in Black patients is associated with an overall greater risk of bleeding complications as well as higher rate of stroke and mortality.14,35 Additionally, some reports noted that that Hispanic patients were less likely to be prescribed OAC than their White counterparts and were more likely to be prescribed warfarin than White patients.20,23,21,25

Our findings confirm and extend evidence of continued racial and ethnic disparities from an earlier systematic review.13 A prior systematic review found that underrepresented racial and ethnic populations are anticoagulated less often for AF than comparable non-Hispanic White patients.13 Given the increasing use of DOACs, our work expands upon those results by examining contemporary research. Our results also confirm that Black individuals are more likely to receive warfarin compared to White individuals who are more often prescribed newer and safer DOACs. This finding is of particular concern as it suggests that Black patients are less likely to receive equitable access to high quality anticoagulant therapy. These demonstrated racial disparities in anticoagulation for AF in real-world practice parallel the underrepresentation of people of color in DOAC trials. A patient level meta-analysis that used the COMBINE AF database, which includes all patients in each of the 4 major DOAC clinical trials, determined that only 1.2% of the combined study population was Black, even though Black people represent 13% of the US population, and only 9.7% of the study population were Hispanic, compared to 16.7% nationally. 36

Several articles found that women were less often prescribed anticoagulation than men, even with higher CHA2DS2-VASc scores. 11,12,37 While this disparity was smaller in magnitude and less consistently demonstrated than racial and ethnic disparities, the findings highlight a need for more equitable prescribing of OAC in women and is consistent with other recent reviews that discuss sex differences in AF.11,12,37 Additionally, utilization of anticoagulation in transgender or non-binary patients with AF is unclear and represents a gap in the research.

Our review also found that the care setting in which AF was diagnosed impacted AF treatment. Patients received different types of OAC when treated in the emergency department versus the outpatient setting versus during an inpatient admission.33 This may be important from a socioeconomic perspective as patients with different financial means may receive clinical care differently.38 It also, however, could simply reflect different care processes in emergency medicine, which is less oriented to longitudinal care. We have included it as a focus of disparities research, since poorer patients are less likely to have health insurance or access to outpatient care, and therefore may be more likely to use the emergency department as their primary source of medical care.38

There are myriad possible mechanisms for the unequal anticoagulation rates observed in this review by race and ethnicity. The mechanisms of these differences are likely related to extrinsic and structural factors rather than genetic or biological factors.15 In the setting of structural bias and underdiagnosis, Black patients with AF are less aware of their diagnosis.39 14 This is likely to lower one’s chance of receiving guideline-directed care. While patient-level trust, including in novel therapies, has often been raised as a mechanism for disparate treatment, prior work does not support this assertion, including the fact that racial disparities in anticoagulation have widened over time, despite long-term available of such therapies to treat AF.16 The role of unconscious bias among individual clinicians is another mechanism that has been understudied and warrants further investigation.16 Understanding the process by which physicians and other providers make decisions regarding OAC prescribing may help elucidate the role that race and ethnicity play in anticoagulation in AF.

Future work should address a broader range of patient populations including indigenous patients, non-English speaking patients, and patients of varying SES.10 Continuing to advance better understanding of mechanisms of these disparities will help achieve pharmacoequity, ensuring that all patients have access to needed medications.40 Alongside a better understanding of mechanisms of disparities in practice, future clinical trials also need to expand enrollment of diverse populations to ensure the external validity of trial results. Promising tactics for improving diversity in trial enrollment include expanding clinical trial locations to diverse and underserved communities, increasing diversity among investigators, continuous community engagement, and providing appropriate data and tech support based on varying levels of access.41

Our results should be interpreted in the setting of certain limitations. First, included studies were heterogeneous, including cohort, case control, and cross-sectional designs. The studies varied with respect to in age distribution, study population size, and ethnicity and race definitions and proportions. Studies were conducted in multiple countries, and therefore likely include differences in populations and medical systems. Second, there is the possibility of missing pertinent studies through our specific search language. Our review methods may have missed additional data on disparities not found within this review if authors did not include pertinent key words in their description. Manuscripts that do not explicitly mention disparities but still contain information about disparities may not have been captured. For example, an analysis describing treatment of AF in American Indian and Alaska Native (AI/AN) patients that does not contain the word “disparity” finds that AI/AN patients have lower odds of OAC compared with non-AI/AN patients (OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.77–0.93). This analysis was not detected by our search string, highlighting the potential for information about disparities to be found in papers not explicitly about disparities. Additionally, our study relied on the PubMed database given its extensive indexing capabilities; however, this may have limited our search results. Finally, as with any review, we cannot detect results that were not published. As such, our aggregate results may reflect publication biases of the underlying literature.

## Conclusion

In this narrative review examining 13 manuscripts published since 2018, we found key disparities in patients with AF who are prescribed anticoagulation. Black race, Hispanic ethnicity, female sex, low education, and low income are frequently associated with less OAC prescription and/or less DOAC utilization. These associations reinforce that disparities have persisted in OAC prescribing patterns in AF. Important hypotheses have been raised to explain the mechanisms of these disparities although further work is needed to develop effective solutions to achieve equity in anticoagulation for patients with AF.
